title: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy
hookLine: a therapy that pairs mindfulness with cognitive therapy to help people step back from their thoughts
last: HONOR THE ANCESTORS AS IF THEY WERE PRESENT.

cards: "I always ruin things." The sentence shows up at two in the morning, fully formed, in your own voice. It has the tone of a fact.
And because it sounds like a fact, the mind starts collecting evidence: that email, that birthday, that thing you said in school. Within minutes there's a whole case file.
After days of practices handed down for a long time, the path turns to a newer room: a clinic. Psychologists there asked a plain question.
What if the trouble isn't only what the thought says, but how tightly we believe it?

teach.b: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, MBCT for short, was developed by three psychologists: Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale.
They joined cognitive therapy, which looks at how thoughts shape mood, with mindfulness practice learned from Jon Kabat-Zinn's stress-reduction courses, which draw on Buddhist meditation.
Their focus was depression that keeps coming back. The idea at the center is decentering.

teach.h: DECENTERING: A THOUGHT IS AN EVENT.
teach.b: Instead of arguing with a dark thought, or obeying it, you learn to see it as a thought: an event in the mind, passing through, like weather. Not the truth about you.
The course puts it in a short phrase: thoughts are not facts. So I always ruin things doesn't get debated. It gets noticed.
Noticing gives a little room, and in that room the case file doesn't have to open. MBCT is taught as a group course, with home practice.
One short exercise, the breathing space, is meant for the middle of an ordinary day: stop, notice what's here, gather attention on the breath, then widen it to the whole body.

Here's what the research honestly showed. In a trial Teasdale and colleagues reported, people who had been through depression several times and took the course were less likely to have it return than those who didn't.
For people with fewer past episodes, the trial didn't find that benefit. It's not a cure-all, and the researchers didn't claim one. MBCT is a therapy, taught by trained teachers.
If you're struggling with depression, a doctor or therapist is the place to start, and if you're ever in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: MBCT is usually taught as a group course led by a trained teacher, with weekly sessions and daily home practice such as guided meditations and the short breathing space, aimed at people who have experienced recurring depression.

notice it as a thought, an event in the mind.
collect evidence to see if it's true.
games.why: MBCT's way is decentering: don't debate or obey the thought. notice it as a thought, and the case file doesn't have to open.

practice: Watch for the next thought that arrives, a plan, a worry, a judgment, and when it comes, put a small label in front of it: I'm having the thought that. I'm having the thought that I'm behind.
Notice the little gap the label makes, then come back to the breath and wait for the next one.

wordCard.voice: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. A course joining cognitive therapy with mindfulness, so people can see thoughts as passing events in the mind, not facts. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: thoughts aren't facts. A thought is weather passing through. I'll be here tomorrow.
